1.why: Tokens are stored globally in recoveries with no user/email binding, so verify never checks that a reset code belongs to a specific user.

2.why: Because tokens are not bound to any user identity, the same reset token can be verified and used from any session that presents it.

3.why: Password reset only updates the in-memory passwordHash and session flags; other existing sessions are never invalidated or removed.

4.why: The app serves over Bun TLS with HTTP→HTTPS redirect and HSTS, but does not explicitly pin or document a specific latest TLS version.

5.why: Passwords are Argon2id-hashed, but reset tokens and flow data sit in plaintext memory maps with no encryption of reset codes or user data.

6.why: The recovery API uses a generic non-enumerating message, yet there is no real email channel and the mock path returns/logs the raw token.

7.why: Inputs are length-limited, email-regex validated, JSON body size-capped, and client output uses textContent/JSON rather than unsanitized HTML.

8.why: Redirects are fixed to https://localhost:${HTTPS_PORT} with no user-controlled redirect targets or open-redirect parameters.

9.why: There are no server email templates that interpolate user input; mock delivery only logs server-generated tokens/codes.

10.why: Reset tokens and MFA codes are written to the on-page Logs panel (and mock API fields), so secrets do appear in logs/UI.

11.why: The MFA secret is hardcoded as "482916" in source, so secret codes are not kept out of the code.

12.why: No default login username/password path or preset credentials are accepted for authentication.

13.why: IP/session rate limits, verify throttling, and mfaFailures >= 5 lockouts block repeated failed attempts.

14.why: Recovery always returns the same generic “If an account can be recovered…” message regardless of whether the email is registered.

15.why: Tokens are cryptographically random 64-hex values, but they are not user-specific because no account identifier is tied to the recovery record.
